why_use_this: This is the broadest statistics toolbox in the vani-* ecosystem -- reach for it for descriptive statistics, probability distributions (PMF/PDF/CDF), correlation and regression, information theory, hypothesis testing (test statistics AND p-values), Bayesian inference, Markov chains, time series analysis, and a few stochastic-process/dimensionality-reduction tools that lean on [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix) (multiple regression, PCA, Kalman filtering). If you need a specific distribution's PDF/PMF and its CDF, they're paired by name (`gamma_pdf`/`gamma_cdf`, `chi_squared_pdf`/`chi_squared_cdf`, ...) -- and where a test statistic exists, its matching p-value function is also paired by name (`t_stat_one_sample` feeds `t_pvalue_two_tailed`, `chi_squared_stat` feeds `chi_squared_pvalue`, ...), so you're rarely more than one function call away from turning a raw statistic into an actual decision. For anything already covered by a compiler builtin (`f64_normal_pdf`/`_cdf`, `rand_normal`, `f64_erf`, `i64_factorial`/`_binomial`, ...) this package deliberately does NOT duplicate it -- call the builtin directly.

math_notes.variance: \( s^2 = \dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2 \) -- the Bessel-corrected (dividing by \( n-1 \), not \( n \)) SAMPLE variance, computed in two passes (mean first, then the sum of squared deviations).
math_notes.std_dev: \( s = \sqrt{s^2} \) -- the square root of `variance`'s Bessel-corrected sample variance.
math_notes.median: The middle value of the sorted sample (or the average of the two middle values for an even-sized sample) -- the 50th percentile, robust to outliers unlike `mean`.
math_notes.skewness: The (Fisher-Pearson) sample skewness \( \dfrac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^3}{s^3} \) -- measures asymmetry: positive means a longer right tail, negative a longer left tail, zero means symmetric (like a normal distribution).
math_notes.kurtosis: The sample kurtosis \( \dfrac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^4}{s^4} \) -- measures tailedness; a normal distribution has kurtosis 3 (this is raw, not "excess", kurtosis, which would subtract 3).
math_notes.weighted_mean: \( \dfrac{\sum_i w_i x_i}{\sum_i w_i} \) -- the arithmetic mean generalized so each observation contributes proportionally to its weight instead of equally.
math_notes.weighted_variance: The weighted analog of `variance`: \( \dfrac{\sum_i w_i(x_i-\bar{x}_w)^2}{W - W_2/W} \) where \( W=\sum w_i \), \( W_2=\sum w_i^2 \), and \( \bar{x}_w \) is `weighted_mean` -- reduces to the ordinary Bessel-corrected `variance` when every weight is 1.
math_notes.quantile: The value below which a fraction \( q \) of the (sorted) sample falls -- `median` is the special case \( q=0.5 \).
math_notes.iqr: \( Q_3 - Q_1 \) (the 75th percentile minus the 25th, both via `quantile`) -- the interquartile range, a robust spread measure less sensitive to outliers than `variance`/`std_dev`.
math_notes.mode: The most frequently occurring value in the sample (after sorting to group equal values together).
math_notes.binomial_pmf: \( P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} \) -- probability of exactly \( k \) successes in \( n \) independent Bernoulli(\(p\)) trials.
math_notes.binomial_cdf: \( P(X \le k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k}\binom{n}{i}p^i(1-p)^{n-i} \) -- the cumulative sum of `binomial_pmf` from 0 to \( k \).
math_notes.poisson_pmf: \( P(X=k) = \dfrac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!} \) -- probability of exactly \( k \) events in a fixed interval, given an average rate \( \lambda \).
math_notes.poisson_cdf: \( P(X \le k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} \dfrac{\lambda^i e^{-\lambda}}{i!} \) -- the cumulative sum of `poisson_pmf` from 0 to \( k \).
math_notes.geometric_pmf: \( P(X=k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p \) -- probability the FIRST success happens on trial \( k \), for i.i.d. Bernoulli(\(p\)) trials.
math_notes.geometric_cdf: \( P(X \le k) = 1-(1-p)^k \) -- closed form, not a summed loop, unlike `binomial_cdf`/`poisson_cdf`.
math_notes.negative_binomial_pmf: \( P(X=k) = \binom{k-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{k-r} \) -- probability the \( r \)-th success happens on trial \( k \), the generalization of `geometric_pmf` (\( r=1 \)) to waiting for \( r \) successes instead of just 1.
math_notes.hypergeometric_pmf: \( P(X=k) = \dfrac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}} \) -- probability of exactly \( k \) successes when drawing \( n \) items WITHOUT replacement from a population of \( N \) containing \( K \) successes (unlike `binomial_pmf`, which assumes independent draws WITH replacement).
math_notes.exponential_pdf: \( f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} \) for \( x \ge 0 \) -- the continuous analog of `geometric_pmf`: time until the next event in a Poisson process with rate \( \lambda \).
math_notes.exponential_cdf: \( F(x) = 1-e^{-\lambda x} \) for \( x \ge 0 \) -- closed form (same formula as `exponential_cdf_exact`; both exist since `exponential_cdf` predates the systematic PDF/CDF-pairing pass that added the `_exact` suffix elsewhere).
math_notes.uniform_pdf: \( f(x) = \dfrac{1}{b-a} \) for \( x \in [a,b] \), else 0 -- constant density over the interval.
math_notes.uniform_cdf: \( F(x) = \dfrac{x-a}{b-a} \) for \( x \in [a,b] \) (0 below \( a \), 1 above \( b \)) -- linear ramp across the interval.
math_notes.t_pdf: The Student's t-distribution density with `df` degrees of freedom -- heavier-tailed than the normal distribution, converging to it as `df` grows; used throughout this package's t-tests (`t_stat_one_sample`/`t_stat_two_sample` feed into `t_cdf`/`t_pvalue_two_tailed`, which use this shape).
math_notes.beta_pdf: The Beta(\(\alpha,\beta\)) distribution density on \( [0,1] \) -- the standard distribution for modeling a probability/proportion itself as a random quantity, e.g. the natural conjugate prior for a binomial's success probability in Bayesian inference.
math_notes.chi_squared_pdf: The chi-squared distribution density with \( k \) degrees of freedom -- the distribution of a sum of \( k \) squared independent standard-normal variables; `chi_squared_stat`'s goodness-of-fit statistic is compared against this distribution via `chi_squared_cdf`/`chi_squared_pvalue`.
math_notes.gamma_pdf: The Gamma(shape, rate) distribution density -- generalizes `exponential_pdf` (the special case shape=1) to the waiting time for MULTIPLE Poisson-process events, not just one.
math_notes.laplace_pdf: \( f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2b}e^{-|x-\mu|/b} \) -- the "double exponential" distribution, symmetric around \( \mu \) with heavier tails than a normal distribution of the same variance.
math_notes.log_normal_pdf: The distribution of a variable whose LOGARITHM is normally distributed with mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \) -- common for modeling quantities that are products of many independent positive factors (by the central limit theorem applied in log-space).
math_notes.covariance: \( \dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y}) \) -- sample covariance, Bessel-corrected like `variance`; positive means \( x \) and \( y \) tend to move together, negative means they tend to move oppositely.
math_notes.pearson_r: \( r = \dfrac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{s_x s_y} \) -- Pearson's correlation coefficient, `covariance` normalized by both standard deviations into \( [-1,1] \); measures LINEAR association only.
math_notes.ols_slope: \( \hat{\beta}_1 = \dfrac{\text{cov}(x,y)}{\text{var}(x)} \) -- the ordinary-least-squares regression slope for simple (one-predictor) linear regression.
math_notes.ols_intercept: \( \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{x} \) -- the OLS intercept, chosen so the fitted line passes through the point of means \( (\bar{x},\bar{y}) \).
math_notes.ols_r_squared: \( R^2 = r^2 \) -- for simple linear regression specifically, the coefficient of determination is exactly Pearson's \( r \) squared (a special-case shortcut; the general multi-predictor version is `mlr_r_squared`).
math_notes.shannon_entropy: \( H(P) = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i \) -- Shannon entropy, the average "surprise"/information content of a distribution; maximized by a uniform distribution, zero for a distribution concentrated on one outcome.
math_notes.kl_divergence: \( D_{KL}(P\Vert Q) = \sum_i p_i \log\dfrac{p_i}{q_i} \) -- Kullback-Leibler divergence, how much information is lost approximating true distribution \( P \) with \( Q \); NOT symmetric (\( D_{KL}(P\Vert Q) \ne D_{KL}(Q\Vert P) \) in general) and not a true distance metric.
math_notes.cross_entropy: \( H(P,Q) = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i = H(P) + D_{KL}(P\Vert Q) \) -- the entropy of \( P \) plus the extra cost of using \( Q \)'s coding scheme instead of \( P \)'s own; the loss function [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `graph_binary_cross_entropy_loss` implements a differentiable-graph version of.
math_notes.renyi_entropy: \( H_\alpha(P) = \dfrac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\sum_i p_i^\alpha \) for \( \alpha \ne 1 \) -- a one-parameter family generalizing `shannon_entropy` (which is the limit as \( \alpha\to 1 \)); different \( \alpha \) values weight rare vs. common outcomes differently.
math_notes.t_stat_one_sample: \( t = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \) -- tests whether a sample's mean differs significantly from a hypothesized value \( \mu_0 \), in units of estimated standard error.
math_notes.t_stat_two_sample: The two-sample t-statistic comparing two independent samples' means, using `pooled_variance` (or the Welch-adjusted degrees of freedom via `welch_df` for unequal variances) in its standard-error denominator.
math_notes.chi_squared_stat: \( \chi^2 = \sum_i \dfrac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i} \) -- the chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic, comparing observed counts \( O_i \) against expected counts \( E_i \) under a null hypothesis.
math_notes.z_stat: \( z = \dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \) -- like `t_stat_one_sample` but assuming the POPULATION standard deviation \( \sigma \) is already known exactly (not estimated from the sample), so it's compared against the normal distribution rather than the t-distribution.
math_notes.conditional_prob: \( P(A\mid B) = P(A\cap B)/P(B) \) -- the definition of conditional probability.
math_notes.law_of_total_prob: \( P(A) = \sum_i P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i) \) -- the law of total probability: an event's overall probability as the weighted sum of its probability under each mutually exclusive, exhaustive scenario \( B_i \).
math_notes.bayes_posterior: Unnormalized Bayes' rule: \( \text{posterior}_i \propto \text{prior}_i \times \text{likelihood}_i \) for each hypothesis \( i \) -- call `normalize_probs` on the result to get an actual probability distribution summing to 1.
math_notes.bayes_log_posterior: The same unnormalized Bayes' rule as `bayes_posterior` but in LOG space (\( \log\text{posterior}_i \propto \log\text{prior}_i + \log\text{likelihood}_i \), addition instead of multiplication) -- avoids numerical underflow when likelihoods are extremely small, the standard trick `naive_bayes_classify` relies on.
math_notes.markov_step: \( \pi'_j = \sum_i \pi_i T_{ij} \) -- one step of a Markov chain: the new state-probability distribution \( \pi' = \pi T \), given the current distribution \( \pi \) and transition matrix \( T \).
math_notes.markov_stationary: Finds the stationary distribution \( \pi^* \) satisfying \( \pi^* = \pi^* T \) (the fixed point of `markov_step`) by iterating `markov_step` from a starting distribution until it stops changing (within `tol`) or `max_iter` is reached -- power iteration applied to a stochastic matrix.
math_notes.markov_tv_distance: \( \delta(\pi,q) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i |\pi_i - q_i| \) -- total variation distance between two probability distributions, used by `markov_mixing_steps` to measure how close a chain has gotten to its stationary distribution.
math_notes.markov_entropy_rate: \( h = -\sum_i \pi_i \sum_j T_{ij}\log T_{ij} \) -- the long-run average entropy (unpredictability) of the chain's next-state transitions, weighted by how often each state \( i \) is visited under the stationary distribution \( \pi \).
math_notes.moving_average: The simple moving average: each output point is the mean of the `window` most recent input points -- smooths short-term fluctuations at the cost of `window`-length lag.
math_notes.ema: The exponential moving average: \( y_t = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)y_{t-1} \) -- weights recent observations more than a simple moving average does, with the weight of an observation \( k \) steps in the past decaying geometrically as \( (1-\alpha)^k \).
math_notes.autocorrelation: \( r_k = \dfrac{\sum_t (x_t-\bar{x})(x_{t+k}-\bar{x})}{\sum_t (x_t-\bar{x})^2} \) -- the correlation of a series with a lagged copy of itself, `pearson_r` applied between \( x_t \) and \( x_{t+k} \); reveals periodicity/persistence in a time series.
math_notes.acf_vec: `autocorrelation` evaluated at every lag from 0 to `max_lag`, returned as one vector -- the full autocorrelation function, typically plotted to spot a series' periodicity.
math_notes.diff_series: \( y_t = x_t - x_{t-1} \) -- first-order differencing, the standard time-series preprocessing step to remove a linear trend and make a series more stationary before further analysis.
math_notes.cumsum: \( y_t = \sum_{i \le t} x_i \) -- the running total; the exact inverse operation of `diff_series` (differencing then cumsum recovers the original series up to the first value).
math_notes.welford_mean_update: Welford's online algorithm's mean-update step: \( \bar{x}_n = \bar{x}_{n-1} + \dfrac{x-\bar{x}_{n-1}}{n} \) -- updates a running mean incrementally, one sample at a time, without storing or re-summing the whole history.
math_notes.welford_m2_update: Welford's algorithm's running sum-of-squared-deviations update: \( M_{2,n} = M_{2,n-1} + (x-\bar{x}_{n-1})(x-\bar{x}_n) \) -- the key numerically-stable trick (uses both the OLD and NEW mean) that lets `welford_variance` compute variance in one streaming pass without the catastrophic cancellation a naive \( \sum x^2 - n\bar{x}^2 \) formula risks.
math_notes.welford_variance: \( s^2 = M_2/(n-1) \) -- recovers the Bessel-corrected sample variance from Welford's running \( M_2 \) accumulator (see `welford_m2_update`), the streaming equivalent of `variance`.
math_notes.f_stat: \( F = s_1^2/s_2^2 \) -- the ratio of two samples' variances, compared against the F-distribution (via `f_cdf`/`f_pvalue`) to test whether the two population variances are equal.
math_notes.pooled_variance: \( s_p^2 = \dfrac{(n_x-1)s_x^2 + (n_y-1)s_y^2}{n_x+n_y-2} \) -- combines two samples' variances into one pooled estimate, weighted by degrees of freedom; assumes the two populations share a common true variance (the assumption `t_stat_two_sample` uses when NOT using Welch's correction).
math_notes.welch_df: \( \dfrac{(s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y)^2}{(s_x^2/n_x)^2/(n_x-1) + (s_y^2/n_y)^2/(n_y-1)} \) -- the Welch-Satterthwaite equation for effective degrees of freedom, used instead of `pooled_variance`'s pooled approach when the two samples' variances can't be assumed equal.
math_notes.standardize: \( z_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/s \) -- z-score standardization of a single vector (the single-vector analog of [vani-ml](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-ml)'s `StandardScaler`, which fits/applies across a whole feature matrix separately).
math_notes.mutual_information_discrete: \( I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log\dfrac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} \) -- how much knowing one discrete variable reduces uncertainty about the other; zero exactly when \( X \) and \( Y \) are independent.
math_notes.chi_squared_cdf: The chi-squared distribution's CDF, evaluated via the regularized incomplete gamma function -- `chi_squared_stat`'s test statistic is looked up against this to get `chi_squared_pvalue`.
math_notes.gamma_cdf: The Gamma(shape, rate) distribution's CDF, via the regularized incomplete gamma function -- the integral of `gamma_pdf`.
math_notes.t_cdf: The Student's t-distribution's CDF -- `t_stat_one_sample`/`t_stat_two_sample`'s statistics are looked up against this (via `t_pvalue_two_tailed`) to get a p-value.
math_notes.beta_cdf: The Beta(\(\alpha,\beta\)) distribution's CDF, via the regularized incomplete beta function -- the integral of `beta_pdf`.
math_notes.f_cdf: The F-distribution's CDF -- `f_stat`'s statistic is looked up against this (via `f_pvalue`) to test equality of variances.
math_notes.t_pvalue_two_tailed: \( p = 2\big(1 - F_t(|t|)\big) \) -- the two-tailed p-value for a t-statistic, via `t_cdf`: the probability of seeing a t-statistic at least this extreme in EITHER direction, under the null hypothesis.
math_notes.chi_squared_pvalue: \( p = 1 - F_{\chi^2}(\text{stat}) \) -- the (one-tailed, since chi-squared statistics are always non-negative and "more extreme" only means "larger") p-value via `chi_squared_cdf`.
math_notes.z_pvalue_two_tailed: \( p = 2\big(1-\Phi(|z|)\big) \) -- the two-tailed p-value for a z-statistic, via the compiler's own `f64_normal_cdf` (\(\Phi\)).
math_notes.f_pvalue: \( p = 1-F_F(\text{stat}) \) -- the p-value for an F-statistic via `f_cdf`.
math_notes.mlr_fit: Ordinary least squares for MULTIPLE predictors: \( \hat{\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty \), the normal-equations solution -- computed via [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_inv_n`, the multi-predictor generalization of `ols_slope`/`ols_intercept`'s simple-regression formulas.
math_notes.mlr_predict: \( \hat{y} = X\hat{\beta} \) -- the fitted model evaluated on (possibly new) data.
math_notes.mlr_r_squared: \( R^2 = 1 - SS_{\text{res}}/SS_{\text{tot}} \) -- the multi-predictor generalization of `ols_r_squared`, computed the general way (from residuals) rather than via the simple-regression `pearson_r`-squared shortcut.
math_notes.mlr_adj_r_squared: \( R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-(1-R^2)\dfrac{n-1}{n-p-1} \) -- adjusts `mlr_r_squared` downward to penalize adding predictors that don't actually improve the fit (plain \( R^2 \) never decreases from adding a predictor, even a useless one; adjusted \( R^2 \) can).
math_notes.cov_matrix: The full covariance matrix \( \Sigma_{ij} = \text{cov}(X_{:,i}, X_{:,j}) \) across every pair of variables (columns) in `X_flat` -- the multivariate generalization of the scalar `covariance` function.
math_notes.correlation_matrix: The full Pearson correlation matrix -- `cov_matrix`'s entries each normalized by their two variables' standard deviations, the multivariate generalization of `pearson_r`.
math_notes.pca_power_iter: Finds the dominant eigenvector of a covariance matrix via power iteration (the same algorithm as [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_eig_power`, specialized to a covariance matrix) -- this is PCA's first principal component: the direction of maximum variance in the data.
math_notes.pca_deflate: Given the found first principal component `pc1`, removes its contribution from the covariance matrix (the same deflation idea as [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_eig_deflate`) so a second call to `pca_power_iter` on the result finds the SECOND principal component instead of re-finding the first.
math_notes.random_walk_1d: Simulates \( x_t = x_{t-1} + \sigma \cdot \xi_t \) for \( n\_steps \) steps, where \( \xi_t \sim N(0,1) \) -- a discrete-time random walk with Gaussian increments scaled by \( \sigma \).
math_notes.geometric_brownian: Simulates geometric Brownian motion: \( S_{t+dt} = S_t \exp\!\big((\mu - \sigma^2/2)dt + \sigma\sqrt{dt}\,\xi_t\big) \), the standard model for a price/quantity that can't go negative and whose PERCENTAGE (not absolute) changes are normally distributed -- the model underlying Black-Scholes option pricing.
math_notes.kalman_predict: The Kalman filter's PREDICT step: projects the state estimate forward one time step, \( \hat{x}' = F\hat{x} \) and its covariance \( P' = FPF^T + Q \), given the state-transition matrix \( F \) and process-noise covariance \( Q \) -- what the system's state is expected to be BEFORE incorporating a new measurement.
math_notes.kalman_update: The Kalman filter's UPDATE step: incorporates a new measurement \( z \) via the Kalman gain \( K = PH^T(HPH^T+R)^{-1} \), correcting the state estimate \( \hat{x} \leftarrow \hat{x} + K(z-H\hat{x}) \) and its covariance \( P \leftarrow (I-KH)P \) -- optimally blends the PREDICTED state (`kalman_predict`'s output) with the new noisy measurement, weighted by their relative uncertainties.
math_notes.spearman_r: Spearman's rank correlation: `pearson_r` computed on the RANKS of the data instead of the raw values -- captures any monotonic relationship (not just linear), so it's more robust than `pearson_r` to outliers and nonlinear-but-monotonic associations.
math_notes.mann_whitney_u_stat: The Mann-Whitney U statistic: a rank-based, nonparametric alternative to `t_stat_two_sample` for testing whether two samples come from the same distribution, without assuming normality.
math_notes.kolmogorov_smirnov_stat: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic: the maximum vertical distance between the two samples' empirical cumulative distribution functions -- a nonparametric test of whether two samples come from the same underlying distribution, sensitive to differences in shape/location/spread all at once.
